newsitem.title: INDIA: Insurgents stalk India's troubled northeast.
newsitem.headline: Insurgents stalk India's troubled northeast.

text.p: Insurgency stalks India's troubled northeast states from all directions but a new good-neighbour policy with Bangladesh could provide some respite, senior inteligence sources told Reuters on Sunday.

Last week, a bomb attack on a train in the main northeast state of Assam killed dozens of people and brought rare attention to the multi-stranded insurgency movements in the vulnerable and remote region.
The train attack was carried out by Bodo tribal militants, just one of many tribal and ethnic guerrilla groups operating in at least five of the seven states.
Most of the unrest appears to have been stirred up by economic neglect and pressure on land from huge influxes of immigrants from Bangladesh and other parts of India.

In Assam, three main groups are operating, the highly organised Bodoland Army, its bitter rival the Bodoland Liberation Tigers Force -- which claimed responsibility for the train attack -- and the United Liberation Front of Assam, an Assamese separatist movement.
In Nagaland, militants among the former headhunting tribes have fought for independence from India ever since the country gained freedom from British rule in 1947.

In the former princely Hindu state of Manipur there are around 15 guerrilla groups belonging to the Meities, highland tribals. Tribals in Tripura and Meghalaya are also fighting because of the loss of land and economic domination by non-tribal newcomers.
Only Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh, on the Chinese border, are peaceful.
The northeast is India's door to Indo-China -- and all that region's convulsions.
The seven states, of which Assam is the largest, are economically backward and geographically almost cut off from the rest of the country by Bangladesh.
"Insurgency has prospered here because of the proximity of international borders, areas the insurgents can get refuge," a top-ranking Indian intelligence officer told Reuters.

India has frontiers in the northeast with Bangladesh, Burma and Bhutan where the guerrillas find sanctuary. There is also the extremely sensitive border with China, but no guerrilla groups operate from there, he said.
The Bhutan and Burmese governments can do little to counter the cross-border movement of insurgents.
The border to the north with Bhutan is largely unadministered, and the Burma's military rulers have lost control of the northern border regions of their country to local guerrilla armies.

Add the money involved in the heroin trade -- which some of India's tribal insurgents are tapping-- from the Golden Triangle and there becomes a rich and complex group of relationships to feed the lawlessness in the region.
The guerrilla groups mainly buy their arms in Bangladesh, which has a flourishing illicit arms bazaar, intelligence sources said.
"Bangladesh has become an important spring, a well for arms. There is a sprawling arms market here with so many groups for customers," the intelligence officer said.
It might be early days for India and Bangladesh's recent move to closer ties, but intelligence sources are hoping the rapprochement will make life more difficult for the insurgents.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda goes to Dhaka on Monday on a two-day visit after last month's ground-breaking Ganges water sharing agreement.
"Right now, Bangladesh has become a more friendly neighbour and put insurgents in a little bit of difficulty," a top-ranking intelligence officer told Reuters.
"The Bangladesh authorities have told us the insurgents are leaving. We have not been able to corroborate that yet. But we have noticed a change in attitude and climate in Bangladesh," he said.
